*   *Para 1:* In the ICI-refractory setting, the MITRIC trial (Phase IIa single-arm) provides a stark counterpoint to first-line optimism. Among 12 patients with advanced solid tumors (melanoma, HNSCC, RCC, pancreatic) progressing on ICIs, FMT from ICI-responders yielded an ORR of 0% [P0578]. Median PFS was merely 1.5 months, with only one patient achieving stable disease beyond 6 months [P0578]. This suggests FMT lacks salvage activity in unselected, rapidly progressing refractory populations.
*   *Para 2:* Mechanistic analysis reveals two barriers. First, engraftment was transient in most recipients; durable donor-recipient similarity was observed only in the single clinical beneficiary [P0578]. Second, the host baseline immune landscape posed a hard barrier. Patients with myeloid-biased environments (high CD14+ monocytes) and elevated serum IL-8 had poorer outcomes, and FMT failed to reverse this myeloid dominance or lower IL-8 levels over time [P0578][P0304]. This aligns with the "ecological pharmacology" view that simply adding exogenous microbes cannot easily overwrite a固化 (solidified) immunosuppressive TME driven by host disease state [P0178][P0474].
*   *Para 3:* Consistent with MITRIC, a prospective single-arm study by Kim et al. in anti-PD-1 refractory solid tumors (mostly upper GI) reported an ORR of only 7.7% and a disease control rate of 46.2% [P0594]. These converging negative/low-response signals in refractory cohorts highlight that FMT is not a universal rescue therapy. Efficacy appears contingent on treatment line (naïve vs. refractory) and the ability to achieve durable engraftment within a permissive immune context, underscoring the need for precision stratification rather than broad application in late-line settings.
